blocks.text: A 79-year-old man develops sudden, severe central abdominal pain and lies rigidly still. His abdomen is board-like. The erect chest radiograph shows a thin crescent of black beneath the right hemidiaphragm. Within minutes a plain film has told you that gas has escaped from the gut, and the next decision is how to image further, and who should operate.

blocks.markdown: **Abdominal imaging is a sequence of choices, not a single test.** For any patient with abdominal pain you ask three things: what is the clinical question (is there perforation, obstruction, an abscess, a stone, a bleed?), who is the patient (a child, a pregnant woman, a frail older adult, an unstable patient?) and what are the harms of each test (ionising radiation, intravenous contrast, delay, transfer out of a monitored area?). In the UK the Royal College of Radiologists *iRefer* guidance supports the referrer, and under the Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations (IR(ME)R) every exposure must be **justified** for that patient, so an ultrasound or MRI that answers the question is preferred over CT when it can.

blocks.title: Pneumoperitoneum (free intraperitoneal gas)
blocks.text: Pneumoperitoneum is gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the bowel lumen. In an adult with an acute abdomen it usually means perforation of a hollow viscus (for example a perforated peptic ulcer) and is a surgical red flag; it can also persist for a few days after laparotomy or laparoscopy, so history matters.

rows: Suspected gallstones, cholecystitis or dilated bile ducts
Fluid-filled gallbladder and ducts are shown very well, no radiation, bedside available
Operator dependent; bowel gas and obesity limit views
Right iliac fossa pain in a child or young woman
Ultrasound first, then escalate per local pathway
Avoids ionising radiation in radiosensitive groups; also screens for ovarian causes
Appendix not always seen; a non-visualised appendix is not a normal result
Suspected renal colic in an adult
Low-dose non-contrast CT (recommended by NICE for adults; pregnant women are assessed with ultrasound)
Most stones are visible on CT without contrast; also shows alternative diagnoses
Radiation; ultrasound shows hydronephrosis but misses many ureteric stones
Acute abdomen with suspected perforation, ischaemia or complicated diverticulitis
CT of the abdomen and pelvis, usually with intravenous contrast
Whole abdomen in seconds; shows small gas volumes, collections and bowel wall enhancement
Radiation, contrast risks, patient must be stable enough to scan

blocks.title: Choosing a first test: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
blocks.prompt: A 35-year-old man has fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Liver blood tests show a cholestatic pattern. Which imaging test should come first and what should you look for?

steps.text: Frame the question. The picture suggests biliary obstruction with possible infection of the bile ducts (cholangitis), so the question is whether the bile ducts are dilated and whether a stone or mass is causing it.

Match test to question. Bile and the gallbladder are fluid-filled, so they appear black (anechoic) against brighter liver on ultrasound. Ultrasound answers the question quickly, at the bedside, without radiation or contrast.

Describe what you look for. A common bile duct wider than the typical upper limit for age (departments differ, and roughly 6 mm in a young adult is often quoted), gallstones with acoustic shadowing, a thick-walled gallbladder, and dilated intrahepatic ducts.

Plan escalation. If ultrasound shows dilated ducts but not the cause, MR cholangiopancreatography or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography may follow; CT is used when a mass, abscess or complication is suspected.

blocks.answer: Ultrasound first: it detects duct dilatation and gallstones without radiation, and the result directs further imaging or endoscopic drainage.

blocks.markdown: **Plain films in the acute abdomen.** Two views are core: an *erect chest radiograph* to look for gas under the diaphragm, and a *supine abdominal radiograph* to assess the bowel gas pattern. Free gas rises, so the patient should sit upright for several minutes before the exposure (local departments set the time); if they cannot, a left lateral decubitus film lets gas collect over the liver edge. Gas outlining both the inner and outer surface of the bowel wall on a supine film is **Rigler sign**, and gas outlining the falciform ligament is another supine sign. A normal plain film does not exclude perforation: CT is far more sensitive for small volumes.

blocks.caption: Sensitivity is the proportion of patients who truly have the disease that a test detects (TP = true positives, FN = false negatives). It is why a plain film or ultrasound that misses disease may need CT as a back-up.

blocks.title: Bowel calibre: the 3-6-9 rule
blocks.text: As a rough guide, small bowel is dilated above about 3 cm, large bowel above about 6 cm and the caecum above about 9 cm (measured on a supine film, ignoring magnification). Small bowel is central with valvulae conniventes that cross the whole lumen; large bowel is peripheral with haustra, folds that do not cross the whole width. These are rules of thumb, not absolute cut-offs.

rows: Central, often stacked like a ladder
Valvulae conniventes cross the full lumen
May be absent with a distal blockage
blocks.caption: Distinguishing small from large bowel obstruction on a supine abdominal film.

blocks.title: Reading an abdominal film in a vomiting patient
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old woman with previous pelvic surgery has vomiting, colicky pain and absolute constipation. A supine abdominal film shows several centrally placed gas-filled loops up to 4 cm wide. Thin folds cross the entire width of each loop. There is no gas in the rectum. What is the likely pattern and what is the next step?

steps.text: Identify the bowel. Central position and folds that cross the whole width are valvulae conniventes, so these are small bowel loops, not colon.
Check the calibre. A diameter of 4 cm exceeds the rough 3 cm threshold, so the small bowel is dilated.
Combine with the clinical picture. Dilated small bowel, no rectal gas, vomiting and previous pelvic surgery (adhesions) give a pattern of small bowel obstruction.

Decide the next step. The film shows the pattern but not the cause or complications. CT with intravenous contrast, used per local pathway, can show the transition point and signs of strangulation or ischaemia. The patient also needs resuscitation and surgical review, which should not wait for imaging.

blocks.answer: The film shows small bowel obstruction; CT is the usual next test to find the cause and look for ischaemia.

blocks.markdown: **Image-guided procedures (interventional radiology).** Interventional radiologists use ultrasound, fluoroscopy or CT to guide needles and catheters through the skin instead of open surgery. Most procedures use the **Seldinger technique**: a needle enters the target, a guidewire passes through it, the needle is removed and a catheter or drain is passed over the wire. Common examples are percutaneous drainage of an abscess or collection, percutaneous nephrostomy to drain an obstructed kidney, percutaneous biliary drainage, and **embolisation**, in which particles or metal coils are delivered through a catheter to block an artery that is bleeding or feeds a tumour. Before any procedure the team confirms the indication and consent, reviews clotting, platelets and anticoagulants against local thresholds, checks allergies and renal function, gives antibiotics where indicated, and plans aftercare.

rows: Collection that is infected and accessible, for example after diverticulitis
Bleeding, bowel injury, sepsis, drain blockage
Active arterial bleeding, for example gastrointestinal bleeding or after trauma; also some tumours
Ischaemia of non-target tissue, access-site complication, contrast reaction
Obstructive jaundice with infection when endoscopic access fails or is unsuitable
blocks.caption: Common image-guided procedures. Details vary by centre.

blocks.title: Following a drain after abscess drainage
blocks.prompt: A drain was placed into an abscess in the left iliac fossa. The nurses record 50 mL, 40 mL and 30 mL in three consecutive 8-hour shifts. What is the 24-hour output, and how is this used?

steps.text: Add the shift volumes. 50 + 40 + 30 = 120 mL over 24 hours.
Interpret the trend. The output falls shift by shift, which supports resolution of the collection when the patient is also clinically improving (falling fever, pain and inflammatory markers).

State how drains are managed. Departments set their own removal rules, often when output is low and the patient is well, sometimes after a repeat imaging check or sinogram. Persistent high output, or sudden cessation with fever, prompts re-imaging for blockage or a residual collection.

blocks.answer: The 24-hour output is 120 mL, falling over time, which is consistent with resolution; removal follows local criteria and clinical review.

blocks.title: Do not delay decompression or send unstable patients away
blocks.text: An obstructed and infected kidney or infected bile duct needs urgent drainage as well as antibiotics. An unstable patient should not travel to a scanner unmonitored; resuscitate first and discuss with radiology the safest imaging route. A normal erect chest radiograph never excludes perforation if the clinical suspicion is high.

points: Match the test to the question and the patient: ultrasound first for biliary disease and for children and pregnant women, low-dose non-contrast CT for adult renal colic, and CT for suspected perforation, ischaemia or complicated disease.
Free gas appears under the diaphragm on an erect chest film or as Rigler sign on a supine abdominal film, but CT is more sensitive.
Small bowel obstruction shows central dilated loops above about 3 cm with valvulae conniventes crossing the lumen; large bowel shows peripheral loops with haustra, above about 6 cm.
Image-guided drainage, nephrostomy and embolisation treat collections, obstruction and bleeding through a needle and catheter, with checks of clotting, consent and aftercare.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has 12 hours of worsening right iliac fossa pain and fever. The surgeons suspect appendicitis. Which imaging approach is most appropriate first?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis straight away

distractorRationale.a: CT is more sensitive but gives radiation to a radiosensitive child, so it is not the first step.
distractorRationale.b: A plain film has low yield for appendicitis and cannot exclude it.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: ultrasound avoids ionising radiation in a child and can show a non-compressible, inflamed appendix.

questions.explanation: In children the lifetime radiation risk per exposure is higher, so ultrasound is the preferred first test for suspected appendicitis, with escalation only if it is non-diagnostic. A plain film cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis, and CT is kept for unresolved cases.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has sudden left loin-to-groin colicky pain and blood in the urine. He is haemodynamically stable. Which first imaging test best fits current UK guidance for adults?

options.text: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the urinary tract

questions.correctOptionText: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the urinary tract

distractorRationale.a: Correct: most stones, including many invisible on plain film, are shown without contrast, and it can reveal alternative diagnoses.
distractorRationale.b: Many stones are radiolucent or hidden by bowel and bone, so a plain film misses them.
distractorRationale.c: Looks for gas under the diaphragm, not a ureteric stone.

questions.explanation: Low-dose non-contrast CT detects most urinary stones and alternative diagnoses and is recommended by NICE for adults with suspected renal colic, subject to local protocols. Pregnant women are instead assessed by ultrasound.

questions.stem: On a supine abdominal radiograph of a patient with severe pain, gas is seen on both sides of the wall of a gas-filled bowel loop, so the wall appears as a thin white line. What is this sign and what does it suggest?

options.text: Valvulae conniventes sign, suggesting small bowel obstruction
Gas-fluid level, suggesting a normal film

distractorRationale.a: Valvulae conniventes are mucosal folds crossing the lumen, a different feature.
distractorRationale.b: Haustra are incomplete folds and do not make the wall visible from both sides.
distractorRationale.c: Gas-fluid levels are not the sign described and do not make the wall visible.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: gas inside and outside the bowel outlines both surfaces of its wall.

questions.explanation: Rigler sign appears when free gas outlines the outer surface of the bowel wall in addition to the intraluminal gas. It indicates pneumoperitoneum, which usually points to perforation, so surgical review and CT follow.

questions.stem: A supine abdominal film shows gas-distended loops framing the periphery of the abdomen, the widest measuring 8 cm. Folds do not cross the whole width of the loops. What is the best interpretation?

distractorRationale.a: Small bowel is central with folds crossing the lumen; the features here do not fit.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: peripheral position, incomplete haustral folds and a calibre above about 6 cm indicate dilated colon.
distractorRationale.c: A calibre of 8 cm is well above normal for colon other than the caecum.
distractorRationale.d: Free gas is gas outside the bowel, not gas inside distended loops.

questions.explanation: Peripheral loops with haustra that do not span the lumen are large bowel, and a diameter of 8 cm exceeds the rough 6 cm threshold. This pattern suggests large bowel obstruction or volvulus, so a cause is sought on CT.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a bleeding peptic ulcer remains unwell after endoscopic treatment fails. CT angiography shows a contrast blush from a branch of the gastroduodenal artery. Which image-guided procedure is most appropriate?

options.text: Transarterial embolisation of the bleeding vessel

questions.correctOptionText: Transarterial embolisation of the bleeding vessel

distractorRationale.a: Drains an obstructed kidney, not a bleeding gastric vessel.
distractorRationale.b: Treats an infected collection; none is described.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: catheter-delivered coils or particles block the bleeding artery.
distractorRationale.d: Drains obstructed bile ducts; ducts are not the problem.

questions.explanation: Embolisation is used when arterial bleeding is shown on CT angiography and endoscopy has failed. The nephrostomy, abscess drain and biliary drain are all drainage procedures and do not stop arterial haemorrhage.

questions.stem: In a study, 120 patients had appendicitis confirmed at surgery. Ultrasound had reported appendicitis in 90 of them. Calculate the sensitivity of ultrasound for appendicitis in this group, as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives). All 120 had the disease and 90 were detected, so sensitivity = 90/120 = 0.75, or 75%. The 30 missed cases are why a negative ultrasound in a patient with ongoing suspicion may be followed by CT or surgical review.

questions.stem: A percutaneous drain reports 66 mL over the last 12 hours, and output has been steady. Estimate the 24-hour output in mL.
questions.explanation: Assuming steady output, the rate is 66/12 = 5.5 mL per hour, so over 24 hours it is 5.5 x 24 = 132 mL. A trend of falling output together with clinical improvement is part of deciding when a drain can be removed.

questions.stem: A woman at 20 weeks of pregnancy has right flank pain and fever. Explain which imaging test you would request first and why, and what you would do if it is inconclusive.
markingGuide: Ultrasound first: no ionising radiation, appropriate in pregnancy
Looks for hydronephrosis, collection or alternative cause
Justification under IR(ME)R and iRefer: choose test without radiation when it can answer the question
Escalate with MRI (or low-dose CT only after specialist discussion if essential) per local pathway
Urgent drainage by nephrostomy or stent if obstructed and infected
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the first-line test because it answers the question without radiation. If it is inconclusive, MRI is preferred and CT is reserved for specialist-agreed situations where the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.

questions.stem: Describe how you would use plain films to assess a patient with suspected bowel perforation and how your interpretation of an abdominal film would differ if the question were bowel obstruction.
markingGuide: Erect chest radiograph (patient upright for some minutes) to look for a crescent of gas under the diaphragm
Supine abdominal film signs of free gas such as Rigler sign and falciform ligament sign
A normal film does not exclude perforation; CT is more sensitive
For obstruction measure calibre: small bowel above about 3 cm, large bowel above about 6 cm, caecum above about 9 cm
Distinguish small from large bowel by position and valvulae conniventes versus haustra
Plain film shows the pattern; CT finds cause and complications
questions.explanation: Perforation is sought by looking for gas that has left the lumen, while obstruction is judged by bowel calibre, distribution and fold pattern. In both situations a plain film is a quick screen and CT is used for confirmation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old patient has a 6 cm infected collection after bowel surgery. Describe the steps and safety checks of image-guided percutaneous drainage and its main risks.
markingGuide: Confirm indication, accessible collection and consent
Check clotting, platelets and anticoagulants and give antibiotics per protocol
Ultrasound or CT guidance, aseptic technique, Seldinger technique with needle, guidewire and drain
Send fluid for microbiology; secure drain and record output
Risks: bleeding, bowel injury, sepsis, drain blockage or displacement
Follow-up: monitor output and clinical response, re-image if no improvement
questions.explanation: Percutaneous drainage reaches the collection through the skin using imaging and the Seldinger technique, with checks before and after the procedure. Risks and aftercare are part of consent and ward care.
